startup.name: Linewise
startup.one_liner: Industrial data layer for physical recursive self improvement
startup.description: Captures how physical things are made, from first design to final assembly, and sells the resulting data to frontier AI and robotics model builders. Buyers are model and robotics labs; revenue model not stated. Team of 25 in San Francisco, Spring 2025 batch.

yc_acceptance.basis: The company is listed in the Spring 2025 batch, so acceptance is already known; this reports the prior. Starting from about 1 percent with a 0.6 to 2 percent band (yc_acceptance.md), raised to 3 percent for the large team and for a physical AI data wedge that matches YC priorities, held below 5 percent because no customers or revenue are stated and data vendor ideas are copyable.
yc_acceptance.why_it_fails: YC would most plausibly decline because the pitch names an ambition (training data for frontier models) but not a buyer, a price or a first customer, and a team of 25 is unusual at application time and raises the question of who is paying them. Data collection companies also look like services businesses with weak defensibility.

anchors.source: python3 -I scripts/base_rates.py --industry Industrials --years 2022-2026 --calibration-only: seed 42% / 48% / 54%, cond 48% (n=23), median 4 months to seed (n=11), seed raises $500K / $3.9M / $5.2M (n=9). B2B 2022-2026: seed 52% cond (n=163).
anchors.adjustment_reason: Set at 1.15 times the 48 percent Industrials anchor, inside the 1.25 cap, because a 25 person team with a clear AI data wedge in a heavily funded sector makes a seed likelier but the winners test showed team size lifts did not separate raisers; named analogs sensei and the robotics data vendor cohort show the sector is crowded. Forecast window: 19.3 months, from 2025-04-07 to 2026-11-17. Seed means a financing round above about $1M from outside investors that closes inside the window; the YC deal does not count. Industrials median is 6 months to seed (p75 22.1) in time_to_milestones.csv, so about 85 to 90 percent of eventual seeds land in this window. These odds do not rank this company against others.

bands.rationale: Small post YC round under $3M, about 20 percent of institutional AI seeds per the winners test shape.
Institutional seed from $3M to $6M, the central band for AI native teams with a live product.
Larger seed from $6M to $12M, where 42 percent of confirmed 2026 raises above $1M fell in the winners test.
Hot category seed above $12M led by a top tier fund.

ladder.why_it_fails: A 25 person team already burns real money, so the seed has to be large and the buyers of its data have to be named. Frontier labs and robotics companies buy data from a few trusted vendors, and Sensei and other data vendors sell the same promise. The most likely miss is that the company cannot show repeat purchases or a data format that foundation model teams actually train on, and investors treat it as a services business with uneven revenue.

anchors.source: python3 -I scripts/base_rates.py --industry B2B --years 2022-2026 --calibration-only: Series A cond 23% (n=84), known only 12%; Industrials 2022-2026 cond 0% (n=11) so far.
anchors.adjustment_reason: Window limited: median months to Series A is 28 (calibration sample) so few companies reach A before month 19, and the conditional rate here counts only A rounds closing inside the same window. Reaching a Series A years later is common for companies with paying customers, so this is not the ever number.

bands.rationale: Thin Series A or extended seed labelled A, below the 2022 and later 25th percentile of $10M.
Central band around the 2022 and later median of $14.2M.
Strong growth round near the 75th percentile of $20M and above.
Breakout lead round for a category leader with fast growth, rare in any cohort of the data.

ladder.why_it_fails: A Series A inside 19 months would need recurring contracts from several robotics or model labs and gross margins above services levels. Data vendors tend to see lumpy, concentrated revenue, and large buyers often build capture in house. Few 2022 and later seed companies have reached A yet (12 percent known only in B2B), so a window reach needs unusual growth.

anchors.source: python3 -I scripts/base_rates.py --calibration-only: Series B given Series A 44 percent known only (n=126), lower and upper bounds 8 and 53 percent unconditional. This is an ever number, not inside the window.
anchors.adjustment_reason: Set about 0.7 times the 44 percent conditional rate because newer batches show only 16 to 23 percent in B2B 2022 and later cohorts so far (right censored). It is an ever figure and is not in the window.

bands.rationale: Down or flat round below the 2022 and later 25th percentile of $25M.
Central band around the 2022 and later median of $37M.
Strong round near the 75th percentile of $57M.
Breakout growth round for a category leader, seen in only a few percent of Series B rounds in the data.

ladder.why_it_fails: Most companies that raise a Series A do not raise a Series B because growth slows against the A plan, burn rises faster than revenue, or the category consolidates around two leaders. Investors at B want repeatable sales or usage economics, and a company that grew on a founder-led motion often cannot show them. Analogs such as the acquired or stalled A stage companies in the cohort show that about half stop here.

anchors.source: python3 -I scripts/base_rates.py --calibration-only: Series C given Series B 36 percent known only (n=55); Series D or later given C 40 percent (n=20). Ever number.
anchors.adjustment_reason: Held at 0.75 times the 36 percent anchor because the cohort is small and late stage data is incomplete; counted ever, years outside the window.

bands.rationale: Thin or down round; Series C medians fell from $64M to $45M between 2018 to 2021 and 2022 and later (n=6 and 9).
Central band near the 2022 and later median of $45M.
Strong growth round for a company that has kept compounding, above the 2022 and later median.
Category leader round, rare and mostly seen for companies that won their market outright.

ladder.why_it_fails: At Series C the bar is a clear path to a very large outcome, so companies fail here when growth decelerates below what a late stage fund underwrites, when a platform owner or a better funded rival wins the category, or when the market stays smaller than the pitch. Only 6 percent of the calibration sample reached C at the known only count, and the survivors mostly had hard to copy distribution or technology.

outcomes.why_it_fails: Data vendors for frontier models can be acquired by a lab or a large annotation company, but concentrated buyers often bring capture in house, and the services margin profile limits valuations. Sensei and later data vendors compete on the same promise, so reaching over $100M needs a data asset that is unique and recurring, not one off projects.

analogs.relevance: Robotics training data collected by paid operators, Summer 2024.
analogs.outcome_summary: Two person company; no verified round beyond aggregator listings and the market of robotics data vendors grew crowded after its batch.

analogs.relevance: Narrow data product the platform owner absorbed.
analogs.outcome_summary: Acquired by GitHub in January 2018 after it launched native alerts, a talent exit.
Home robot company by Apple alumni; a peer in the physical AI funding wave, no priced institutional round found for it.

killers.risk: Concentrated buyers: a handful of labs buy data and can build capture in house, so revenue is lumpy and renewals uncertain.
killers.evidence: Robotics data demand rests on a few labs; market commentary notes annotation and labelling are bottlenecks that large vendors such as iMerit also sell.
killers.mitigation: Sign multi year data agreements with two labs and own a format or manufacturing partnerships that rivals cannot get.

killers.risk: Services economics: with 25 people on payroll the company looks like a data collection services firm with low margins.
killers.evidence: Capturing assembly and design data needs on site access and operators, so cost scales with volume unless tools are automated.
killers.mitigation: Productize capture with wearable or software tools and show gross margin above 60 percent.

killers.risk: Access: factories restrict sensitive process data, so exclusive manufacturing partners are hard to win and keep.
killers.evidence: Manufacturers guard process knowledge and IP, so data licensing needs contracts that the founders have not shown.
killers.mitigation: Start with partners who gain from the data such as contract manufacturers.

competition_now.name: Sensei
competition_now.what: Robotics training data collected by paid operators.
competition_now.traction: Two person Summer 2024 YC company, no confirmed round.

competition_now.name: iMerit
competition_now.what: Wearable camera egocentric capture and annotation for embodied AI.
competition_now.traction: Established annotation vendor marketing to the same buyers.

competition_now.name: In house capture at robotics labs
competition_now.what: Labs teleoperate and record their own data.
competition_now.traction: The default for most robotics labs, per vendor and commentary sources.

technical_complexity.rationale: Capturing multimodal assembly data, aligning it to CAD and design and producing training grade labels is hard engineering work, but not frontier research. A team of 25 can build capture tooling in months; the risk lies in data quality that models actually benefit from and in access to factories.

who: Robotics labs building capture in house
takeover_risk.rationale: Annotation incumbents already sell similar capture services and labs can build it themselves, so the wedge can be copied within a year. Defensibility comes from exclusive partnerships with manufacturers and from the dataset itself, neither of which is stated.

evidence.claim: Commentary and vendors report robotics labs buying large amounts of egocentric human video for pretraining, though evidence is largely vendor material.
Annotation of first person footage with hand pose and task labels is a bottleneck, which supports demand for structured industrial data.

roadmap.goal: A named buyer and a priced pilot.
actions: Sign a paid pilot with one robotics or model lab.
Capture one full assembly process end to end.
roadmap.proof: A purchase order for a data package.

roadmap.goal: Repeat revenue from at least two buyers with improving margin.
actions: Renew or expand the first buyer and win a second.
Automate capture to cut cost per hour of data.
roadmap.proof: Annualized revenue above $1M with gross margin above 50 percent.

roadmap.goal: Exclusive data access and recurring contracts.
actions: Move from project fees to multi year licences.
roadmap.proof: Over 70 percent of revenue under multi year contracts.

pros.point: A large team already building at application time, with a clear buyer type in AI labs.
pros.evidence: Team size is 25 per the input and the stated buyers are frontier AI and robotics model builders.

pros.point: Physical AI data is a funded category.
pros.evidence: Industrials 2022 and later cohort reaches seed at 48 percent known only with median 4 months (n=11), per base_rates.py.

brand.name: Linewise
brand.name_check: python3 -I scripts/name_features.py --score "Linewise" --era 2022+: kind suffix_coinage, 8 characters, cohort alive 91.0% (n=133)
weaknesses: Descriptive suffix coinage similar to many B2B names
brand.rationale: The name points at manufacturing lines and is fine for an industrial B2B vendor, though it says nothing about AI data. Suffix coinages in the name data (n=133) show slightly lower survival than average, which is confounded with industry, so brand moves nothing in the ladder.

narrative.headline: A large, ambitious team in the hottest physical AI data category with no stated buyer: seed odds near the anchor, but the pitch is a vendor to few buyers.
narrative.general_summary: Linewise wants to capture how things are made and sell that as training data for frontier models and robotics. The team of 25 and the hot category make a seed above $1M in the 19 month window more likely than for a typical company: the Industrials cohort reached seed at 48 percent known only, and the estimate here is 55 percent, inside the 1.25 cap. Series A in the window is less likely because data vendors have concentrated buyers and services margins, and Sensei and iMerit already sell similar capture. The data asset, not the capture service, determines whether the company becomes valuable.

assumptions: Description only; no customers or revenue stated.
Window is 19.3 months; Series B and C are ever figures outside it.
One web result was dated June 2026 and was ignored; no result named Linewise.
